headline: Merz's party falls to 5% in a German state election
summary: Exit polls put Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats at 5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, the party's worst state result since World War II. The far-right AfD led there with 38%. In Berlin the CDU came second to the Left. Merz called it a disaster, said he will stay on, and dropped his trip to the UN next week.

cover_question.q: Do you have to quit if you lose?

cover_answer: No. Merz says he's staying. Eight state leaders back him.
table_question: After a big loss, do you change the plan or push harder?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Germany picked new leaders for two of its states on Sunday, and the party of the man who runs the whole country got 5 votes out of every 100. That's one kid in a class of 20. He says he's staying in his job anyway. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: One number turned into a classroom. Five in a hundred is a thing they can see.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them one: five in a hundred, one kid in a class of 20. Chancellors, states and the AfD stay out. Expect “is he sad?” Yes, he called it a disaster. Then he said he's staying, which is the part to leave them with.

8-12.script: Germany's states elect their own parliaments, like states here electing governors. On Sunday Merz's party got 5% in one and second in Berlin, two weeks after losing a third to the far-right AfD. Three losses in a row, and the coach keeps the playbook: his reforms come anyway, he says.
8-12.why: Three elections and a coach who keeps the playbook. Kids this age can judge that call.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults change course when things go wrong, so the script hands them the chain: three state losses in a row, and a leader who keeps the playbook. Expect “shouldn't he quit?” Say some in his party think so, and eight state leaders said no. Let them make the call.

13-17.script: Voters handed Merz's party 5%. Change course or hold it? He says the loss makes his reforms more urgent. Second: the AfD won a state with 38% and still won't govern, since no other party will work with it. Democracy working, or voters overruled?
13-17.why: Two disputes, no verdict. Let them argue the AfD point first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the AfD won a state, and it still won't govern. The script asks whether that is the system working or the voters overruled, and lets them argue it before you do. Expect “what would you do?” Answer honestly, then ask what they would want said about the losing side.

5-7.a: No. Germany's states each pick their own leaders. His job is a different one, and he says he's keeping it.

8-12.q: Do you have to quit if you lose?
8-12.a: No. Merz says he's staying, and eight state leaders backed him this week.
Against migration and friendly to Russia. Other parties won't work with it.

13-17.q: Why won't anyone work with the AfD?
13-17.a: AP calls it anti-migration and Russia-friendly. No party will partner with it.

13-17.q: Is he going to get replaced?
13-17.a: Maybe. Some in his party want a swap, and he skipped the UN trip.
